When Can We Trust LLM Graders? Calibrating
Confidence for Automated Assessment
Robinson Vasquez Ferrer, Damla Turgut,
Zhongzhou Chen, and Shashank Sonkar
University of Central Florida
{robinson.vasquezferrer, shashank.sonkar}@ucf.edu
Abstract.LargeLanguageModels(LLMs)showpromiseforautomated
grading, but their outputs can be unreliable. Rather than improving
grading accuracy directly, we address a complementary problem:predict-
ing when an LLM grader is likely to be correct. This enables selective au-
tomation where high-confidence predictions are processed automatically
while uncertain cases are flagged for human review. We compare three
confidence estimation methods (self-reported confidence, self-consistency
voting, and token probability) across seven LLMs of varying scale (4B
to 120B parameters) on three educational datasets: RiceChem (long-
answer chemistry), SciEntsBank, and Beetle (short-answer science). Our
experimentsrevealthatself-reportedconfidenceconsistentlyachievesthe
best calibration across all conditions (avg ECE 0.166 vs 0.229 for self-
consistency). Surprisingly, self-consistency remains 38% worse despite re-
quiring 5×the inference cost. Larger models exhibit substantially better
calibration though gains vary by dataset and method (e.g., a 28% ECE
reduction for self-reported), with GPT-OSS-120B achieving the best cal-
ibration (avg ECE 0.100) and strong discrimination (avg AUC 0.668).
We also observe that confidence is strongly top-skewed across methods,
creating a “confidence floor” that practitioners must account for when
setting thresholds. These findings suggest that simply asking LLMs to
report their confidence provides a practical approach for identifying re-
liable grading predictions. Code is available here.
Keywords:Large Language Models, Automated Grading, Confidence Calibra-
tion, Automated Assessment, Human-AI Collaboration, Short Answer Grading,
Long Answer Grading
1 Introduction
LargeLanguageModels(LLMs)areincreasinglyusedforautomatedgrading,but
their reliability remains questionable. Studies have found that GPT-4 produces
scores that differ from human evaluators [20] and makes common arithmetic
errors that reduce accuracy to 20% on complex problems [12]. While LLMs can
match human agreement on some dimensions, they achieve only fair agreement
on others [32], and performance degrades substantially for low-quality studentarXiv:2603.29559v1  [cs.CL]  31 Mar 2026

2 R. Ferrer et al.
work [33]. These limitations raise a fundamental question:when can we trust an
LLM’s grading decision?
Rather than attempting to improve grading accuracy directly, we address a
complementary problem:predicting when an LLM grader is likely to be correct.
Thisframingenablesselectiveautomation,wherehigh-confidencepredictionsare
processedautomaticallywhileuncertaincasesareflaggedforhumanreview.Such
human-AI collaboration can preserve grading quality while reducing instructor
workload on the cases where LLMs are reliable.
The key to effective selective automation isconfidence calibration: a confi-
dence score of 0.8 should correspond to 80% accuracy among predictions at that
confidence level. Well-calibrated confidence enables principled decisions about
when to trust automated grading. Unfortunately, modern neural networks tend
to be poorly calibrated, often exhibiting systematic overconfidence [14], and
this problem persists in LLMs [35]. Recent surveys have catalogued various ap-
proaches to confidence estimation and calibration in LLMs [13].
We systematically evaluate three approaches to confidence estimation, each
groundedinfoundationalNLPresearch:sampling-basedconsistencychecks(self-
consistency) [34], prompting the model to verbalize its uncertainty (self-reported
confidence) [18], and leveraging internal probability mass over “yes”/“no” verdict
tokens (token probability) [21].
We evaluate these methods across seven LLMs spanning two orders of magni-
tude in scale (4B to 120B parameters): Llama-8B/70B [29], Qwen-4B/80B-A3B
variants [30], and GPT-OSS-20B/120B [25]. We test on three established educa-
tional datasets: RiceChem for long-answer chemistry grading [28], and SciEnts-
BankandBeetleforshort-answerscienceassessment[5].Ourprimarycalibration
metrics are Expected Calibration Error (ECE) and the Brier score, which to-
gether measure how well confidence scores predict accuracy.
Our experiments yield several findings with practical implications:
– Self-reported confidence achieves the best calibration.Across all six
evaluated conditions, simply prompting the models to state their confidence
outperforms sampling-based alternatives. Despite requiring higher inference
cost, self-consistency performs worse than self-reported.
– Model scale boosts accuracy more than calibration.Larger models
are consistently more accurate across all three datasets, while calibration
gains are mixed and dataset/method-dependent. We report detailed per-
dataset calibration changes and per-model comparisons in Results.
– Confidence is top-skewed across methods.Confidence distributions
are heavily concentrated at high values; self-consistency is discrete by con-
struction, while self-reported and token-probability are continuous. These
distributions create practical confidence floors, so thresholds should be set
relative to each model/method’s observed scores rather than an intuitive
midpoint.
These findings suggest that simply asking LLMs to report their confidence
provides a practical approach for identifying reliable grading predictions. With

Calibrating LLM Confidence for Automated Assessment 3
appropriate threshold calibration relative to the model’s confidence distribution,
selectiveautomationcanprocesshigh-confidencepredictionsautomaticallywhile
flagging uncertain cases for human review.
2 Related Work
2.1 Calibration of Neural Networks
Calibration, the correspondence between predicted confidence and actual accu-
racy, has been extensively studied in the machine learning literature. Early work
established foundational calibration methods: [27] introduced Platt scaling us-
ing sigmoid functions to calibrate SVM outputs, while [36] proposed isotonic
regression as a non-parametric alternative. [14] demonstrated that modern deep
neural networks are poorly calibrated, typically exhibiting overconfidence, and
proposed temperature scaling as a simple post-hoc method. [15] showed that
maximum softmax probability serves as a baseline for detecting misclassified
examples, though it remains imperfect. For language models specifically, [31]
demonstrated that RLHF-trained models like GPT-4 produce verbalized confi-
dence that is often better calibrated than internal probabilities. In this work, we
focus on eliciting confidence from LLMs rather than applying post-hoc calibra-
tion.
2.2 Confidence Estimation in NLP
Several approaches have been proposed for estimating uncertainty in LLM out-
puts. [34] introduced self-consistency, which samples multiple reasoning paths
and takes a majority vote; the agreement level provides a natural confidence
measure. [21] proposed semantic entropy, which clusters sampled responses by
meaning before computing uncertainty, providing a principled measure that is
invariant to paraphrasing.
Ensemble-based methods offer another paradigm: [23] showed that deep en-
sembles provide well-calibrated uncertainty estimates, while [11] demonstrated
that MC Dropout approximates Bayesian inference for uncertainty estimation.
However, these methods require multiple forward passes or model copies, which
is prohibitive for large language models.
Self-reported confidence, explicitly prompting models to state their confi-
dence, has emerged as a lightweight alternative. [18] demonstrated that language
models “mostly know what they know,” exhibiting metacognitive capabilities.
2.3 Automated Short Answer Grading
Automated Short Answer Grading (ASAG) has a rich history in educational
data mining. The SciEntsBank and Beetle datasets, introduced by [6] and for-
malized as a shared task [5], have served as standard benchmarks. [3] provided
a comprehensive survey identifying 35 ASAG systems across five temporal eras.

4 R. Ferrer et al.
The emergence of LLMs has transformed ASAG research. [17] showed that
GPT-4canachievesubstantialagreementwithhumangraders(quadraticweighted
kappaof0.68)withouttask-specifictraining.Forlong-answergrading,theRiceChem
dataset formulates the task as rubric entailment [28].
While this prior work focuses on improving grading accuracy, our work ad-
dresses the complementary problem of predicting when automated grades are
reliable. This confidence-aware perspective enables practical deployment with
appropriate human oversight.
3 Methodology
We formalize the grading task and then describe three methods for estimating
confidence in LLM grading predictions. We consistently prompt the model to
emit a JSON dictionary whose ‘"verdict"‘ key holds the yes/no grading decision;
all confidence methods operate on that verdict plus derived uncertainty signals.1

3.3 Evaluation Metrics
Expected Calibration Error (ECE)[26]
ECE measures the average difference between confidence and accuracy across
confidence bins:
ECE=BX

whereB bis the set of predictions in binb, acc(B b)is the accuracy within the bin,
and conf(B b)is the mean confidence. Lower ECE indicates better calibration.
We useB= 10equal-width bins.

The Brier score measures mean squared error between confidence and binary

Lower Brier scores indicate better calibration and discrimination combined.
AUC-ROCTheAreaUndertheROCCurvemeasuresrankingquality—whether
higher confidence corresponds to higher accuracy. AUC-ROC ranges from 0.5
(random) to 1.0 (perfect ranking). [8]
Coverage at RiskFor practical deployment, we report coverage at fixed risk
thresholds: the fraction of predictions that can be automated while maintaining
accuracy above a target level.
Statistical MethodsWe report 95% confidence intervals for all primary met-
rics using a student-block bootstrap (1,000 draws, percentile intervals). Each
bootstrap sample resamples students with replacement and keeps all of that stu-
dent’s responses together, preserving within-student dependence.[9,7] To assess
feature–calibration interactions, we fit linear mixed-effects models with random
intercepts for students, answers and rubrics, and report standardized coefficients
(β). Question effects are modeled as fixed effects for small question sets (≤20)
and as random intercept otherwise. [10,24,4] We extract features from rubrics,
student answers, LLM responses, and question text. We also run paired boot-
strap comparisons on identical instances to test method/model dominance.[19]
We control false discovery rate using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure.[1]
Interpretation.We treat claims supported by paired comparisons and confi-
dence intervals as inferential (expected to generalize to similar ASAG tasks with
comparable prompts, rubrics, and response distributions).

Calibrating LLM Confidence for Automated Assessment 7
4 Experiments and Results
4.1 Experimental Setup
Datasets.We evaluate on three educational datasets covering different domains
and answer lengths.RiceChem[28] contains long-answer chemistry questions
requiring explanations, with 8,392 student responses across 4 questions and 27
rubric items.SciEntsBank[5] provides short-answer science questions; in our
experiments it includes 10,804 responses across 200 questions.Beetle[5] con-
tains short-answer questions about electronics and circuits with 3,559 responses
across 56 questions and an average answer length of about 10 words. Each in-
stance consists of a question, student response, rubric item, and binary correct-
ness label.
Models.We evaluate seven LLMs spanning two orders of magnitude in pa-
rametercount.Smallmodels(<20Bparameters)includeLlama-3.1-8B-Instruct[29],
Qwen3-4B-Thinking [30], and GPT-OSS-20B [25].Large models(≥70B param-
eters) include GPT-OSS-120B [25], Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct [29], Qwen3-Next-
80B-A3B-Thinking, and Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct [30]. The Qwen3-80B
variants allow comparison between standard instruction-following and extended
thinking modes within the same architecture.
Implementation Details.All experiments use the vLLM backend with
nucleus sampling [16,22]. Large models run on four NVIDIA A100 GPUs with
tensor parallelism, while small models execute on a bench-top GeForce RTX
3090. Sampling parameters follow model card recommendations (temperature
0.6–0.7, top-p0.8–0.95, top-k20 where applicable). We set maximum generation
length to 8,192 tokens for large models and 30,000 tokens for small models,
and batch sizes to 16 (large) and 128 (small). Models return JSON-formatted
verdicts;self-consistencyusesn= 5andmajorityvote.Wereportrawconfidence
scores throughout.
4.2 Main Results
Tables 1 and 2 summarize results averaged across models within each size cat-
egory. We compute percentile bootstrap confidence intervals by repeatedly re-
sampling students with replacement; typical CI widths are ECE≈0.014–0.057
and Brier≈0.010–0.046 (medians 0.021 and 0.019).
Finding 1: Self-reported confidence achieves the best calibration.
Across all six conditions (3 datasets×2 model sizes), self-reported confidence
consistently achieves the lowest Expected Calibration Error (ECE). Averaged
across datasets, self-reported confidence achieves ECE of 0.197 for small models
and 0.142 for large models. The corresponding ECE values for self-consistency
are0.240/0.221andfortokenprobability0.226/0.242.Overall,self-reportedECE
averages 0.166, compared to 0.229 for self-consistency and 0.235 for token prob-
ability; overall Brier follows the same ordering (0.223 vs 0.241 and 0.244).
Paired bootstrap comparisons on identical responses (Table 3) show median
deltas favoring self-reported in every dataset. Median paired CIs exclude zero.

4.3 Calibration Visualization
To visualize calibration behavior, Figure 1 shows calibration curves (left) and
confidence histograms (right) for GPT-OSS-120B with self-reported confidence
across all three datasets. SciEntsBank tracks the diagonal most closely (low-
est ECE/Brier), while RiceChem and Beetle are slightly less calibrated (higher
ECE/Brier). The histograms are top-skewed with most mass above 0.8 and vir-
tually none below 0.2, so thresholds should be calibrated to observed confidence
distributions rather than a fixed midpoint.
4.4 Per-Model Analysis
To explain the size-averaged trends, we examine model-specific patterns. Table 5
shows results for individual large models with self-reported confidence.
Qwen3-80B: Thinking vs Instruct tradeoff.Comparing Qwen3-80B-
Thinking with Qwen3-80B-Instruct reveals a clear tradeoff between accuracy
andcalibration.OnRiceChem,thethinkingvariantachievessubstantiallyhigher
accuracy (77.5% vs 71.7%, a 5.8 percentage point gain) with better calibration
(ECE 0.142 vs 0.197; Brier 0.187 vs 0.240), suggesting that extended reasoning
helps with complex chemistry explanations. In contrast, on the short-answer
datasets the thinking variant’s calibration is weaker (SciEntsBank ECE/Brier
0.161/0.198 vs 0.126/0.198; Beetle 0.198/0.233 vs 0.132/0.205), which might
come occasional overconfidence when longer reasoning paths miss simpler cues.
GPT-OSS-120B: Best calibration with stable reasoning.Under self-
reported confidence, GPT-OSS-120B achieves average ECE of 0.100, average

Brier of 0.180, and average AUC of 0.668 across all three datasets, substan-
tially outperforming other large models under self-reported confidence (avg ECE
0.157, avg Brier 0.209, avg AUC 0.615). This represents 36% lower ECE, 14%
lower Brier, and 9% higher AUC. Table 6 shows GPT-OSS-120B performance
across reasoning levels (high, medium, low). Unlike Qwen’s large variation be-
tween thinking modes, GPT-OSS-120B exhibits remarkable stability: accuracy
varies by at most 1.2 percentage points and ECE by at most 0.009 across reason-
ing levels. On SciEntsBank, all three reasoning levels achieve identical accuracy
(79.1%) with ECE ranging only from 0.081 to 0.085. This stability suggests that
GPT-OSS-120B’s calibration quality is robust to reasoning depth, making it a
reliable choice for deployment without careful tuning of reasoning parameters.
4.5 Practical Implications
For deployment, well-calibrated confidence enables selective automation, where
high-confidence predictions are processed automatically while uncertain cases
are flagged for human review. With GPT-OSS-120B on SciEntsBank, Cover-
age@10%Risk is about 20% and Coverage@5%Risk is 11.5%; the highest Cov-
erage@5%Risk we observe is 19.5% (Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, self-reported, Sci-
EntsBank). This also sets a practical limitation: even at 5% risk, only about
11%–20% of predictions qualify in our best-performing runs, so selective au-
tomation covers a modest share under strict reliability targets.
5 Conclusion
WeevaluatedwhichconfidencesignalcanbesttelluswhenanLLMgraderisreli-
able, comparing self-consistency, self-reported confidence, and token-probability
estimates across seven models and three educational datasets. This work keeps
experimental conditions (prompts, rubrics, student populations) consistent so
the comparisons are directly comparable and the calibration statistics are inter-
pretable. Finding 1: Self-reported confidence yields the most calibrated signal
within these ASAG settings, outperforming sampling-based alternatives while
keeping inference cost low. Finding 2: Larger models deliver steadier accuracy
gains, but calibration improvements remain dataset- and method-dependent.
Finding 3: Confidence scores are top-skewed, so thresholds should be set relative
to each method’s observed distribution rather than an intuitive midpoint. Taken
together, these results support using self-reported confidence as the automation
gate while recognizing that strict reliability targets cover only a modest share of
predictions. Mixed-model and paired-bootstrap analyses provide the statistical
backing that makes this practical guidance trustworthy.

structure.title: Introduction
structure.summary:
This partial document discusses the reliability of Large Language Models (LLMs) for automated grading. The main points covered are:

*   **The Problem:** LLMs show promise for automated grading but their outputs can be unreliable, leading to questions about when their grading decisions can be trusted.
*   **Proposed Solution:** Instead of directly improving grading accuracy, the research focuses on predicting *when* an LLM grader is likely to be correct. This enables selective automation, where high-confidence predictions are processed automatically, and uncertain cases are flagged for human review.
*   **Confidence Estimation Methods:** The study compares three methods for estimating LLM confidence:
    *   Self-reported confidence (prompting the LLM to state its confidence).
    *   Self-consistency voting (sampling multiple reasoning paths and taking a majority vote).
    *   Token probability (leveraging internal probability mass over verdict tokens).
*   **Experimental Setup:** These methods are evaluated across seven LLMs of varying scales (4B to 120B parameters) on three educational datasets: RiceChem (long-answer chemistry), SciEntsBank, and Beetle (short-answer science).
*   **Key Findings:**
    *   **Self-reported confidence is the most effective:** It consistently achieves the best calibration across all tested conditions, outperforming self-consistency despite lower inference costs.
    *   **Model scale improves calibration:** Larger LLMs generally exhibit better calibration, though the gains vary by dataset and method.
    *   **Confidence is top-skewed:** Confidence scores tend to be concentrated at high values, creating a "confidence floor" that practitioners need to consider when setting thresholds for automation.
*   **Implication:** Simply asking LLMs to report their confidence is a practical approach for identifying reliable grading predictions, facilitating human-AI collaboration in automated assessment.

structure.title: Related Work
structure.summary:
This partial document discusses the calibration of confidence scores for Large Language Models (LLMs) in automated assessment. It highlights the importance of calibrating LLM confidence to enable selective automation, where high-confidence predictions are processed automatically and uncertain cases are flagged for human review. The document then delves into related work, covering:

*   **Calibration of Neural Networks:** Discusses foundational calibration methods like Platt scaling and isotonic regression, the overconfidence issue in deep neural networks and temperature scaling as a solution, and the limitations of maximum softmax probability. It also notes that RLHF-trained models like GPT-4 can have better verbalized confidence than internal probabilities.
*   **Confidence Estimation in NLP:** Explores techniques such as self-consistency (majority voting on multiple reasoning paths), semantic entropy (clustering responses by meaning), and ensemble-based methods (deep ensembles, MC Dropout). It also mentions self-reported confidence as a lightweight alternative, suggesting LLMs have metacognitive abilities.
*   **Automated Short Answer Grading (ASAG):** Briefly touches upon the history of ASAG, mentioning benchmark datasets like SciEntsBank and Beetle, and a survey of ASAG systems.

structure.title: Methodology
structure.summary: This partial document discusses the application of Large Language Models (LLMs) in automated essay grading (ASAG). It highlights that LLMs like GPT-4 can achieve significant agreement with human graders without specific training. The document then shifts focus from improving grading accuracy to a complementary problem: predicting the reliability of automated grades. This "confidence-aware" approach is presented as crucial for practical deployment with human oversight. The methodology section formalizes the grading task as a binary classification problem (satisfies rubric item or not) and introduces three methods for estimating confidence in LLM grading predictions. These methods operate on the LLM's grading decision and derived uncertainty signals, aiming to estimate the probability that the LLM's prediction matches the true grading outcome.

nodes.title: Evaluation Metrics
nodes.summary:
This partial document describes the evaluation metrics and experimental setup for assessing the calibration of Large Language Models (LLMs) in automated assessment tasks.

**Main points covered:**

*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **Expected Calibration Error (ECE):** Measures the discrepancy between predicted confidence and actual accuracy across confidence bins. Lower ECE indicates better calibration.
    *   **Brier Score:** Measures the mean squared error between confidence and binary correctness. Lower Brier scores indicate better combined calibration and discrimination.
    *   **AUC-ROC:** Evaluates the ranking quality of confidence scores, indicating whether higher confidence correlates with higher accuracy.
    *   **Coverage at Risk:** Reports the fraction of predictions that can be automated while maintaining accuracy above a target level, relevant for practical deployment.
*   **Statistical Methods:**
    *   **Confidence Intervals:** 95% confidence intervals are reported using a student-block bootstrap method to account for within-student dependence.
    *   **Linear Mixed-Effects Models:** Used to assess feature-calibration interactions, with random intercepts for students, answers, and rubrics.
    *   **Feature Extraction:** Features are extracted from rubrics, student answers, LLM responses, and question text.
    *   **Paired Bootstrap Comparisons:** Used to test method/model dominance.
    *   **False Discovery Rate Control:** The Benjamini–Hochberg procedure is employed.
    *   **Interpretation:** Claims supported by paired comparisons and confidence intervals are treated as inferential.
*   **Experimental Setup:**
    *   **Datasets:** Evaluation is performed on three educational datasets: RiceChem (long-answer chemistry), SciEntsBank (short-answer science), and Beetle (short-answer electronics/circuits).
    *   **Models:** Seven LLMs are evaluated, categorized into small (<20B parameters) and large (≥70B parameters), including variants of Llama, Qwen, and GPT-OSS.
    *   **Implementation Details:** Specifies the vLLM backend, nucleus sampling, hardware used, sampling parameters (temperature, top-p, top-k), maximum generation length, batch sizes, and the use of JSON-formatted verdicts and self-consistency with majority vote. Raw confidence scores are reported.
*   **Main Results (Preliminary):**
    *   **Finding 1:** Self-reported confidence consistently achieves the best calibration (lowest ECE and Brier scores) across datasets and model sizes, outperforming self-consistency and token probability methods. Paired bootstrap comparisons support this finding.

nodes.title: Main Results
nodes.summary:
This partial document describes an experiment evaluating the calibration of Large Language Model (LLM) confidence for automated assessment. The main points covered are:

*   **Experimental Setup:**
    *   **Datasets:** Three educational datasets (RiceChem, SciEntsBank, Beetle) with varying question types and answer lengths were used. Each instance includes a question, student response, rubric item, and correctness label.
    *   **Models:** Seven LLMs were evaluated, categorized into small (<20B parameters) and large (≥70B parameters), including variants of Llama, Qwen, and GPT-OSS.
    *   **Implementation Details:** Specific hardware, software (vLLM backend), sampling parameters, generation lengths, and batch sizes are detailed. Confidence scores are reported raw, and self-consistency uses n=5 with majority vote.

*   **Main Results:**
    *   **Finding 1: Self-reported confidence achieves the best calibration.** Across all datasets and model sizes, self-reported confidence consistently yielded lower Expected Calibration Error (ECE) and Brier scores compared to self-consistency and token probability methods.
    *   **Finding 2: Model scale boosts accuracy more than calibration.** Larger models generally showed higher accuracy, but calibration improvements with scale were mixed and method-dependent.
    *   **Finding 3: Confidence is top-skewed across methods.** The majority of confidence scores, especially for self-reported and token probability methods, were high (above 0.8), suggesting that assessment thresholds should be set relative to observed distributions.

*   **Calibration Visualization:** Calibration curves and confidence distributions for a specific model (GPT-OSS-120B) are presented, illustrating overconfidence and the top-skewed nature of confidence scores.

*   **Per-Model Analysis:**
    *   Individual large model performance is analyzed, highlighting GPT-OSS-120B's strong calibration.
    *   A trade-off between accuracy and calibration is observed for Qwen3-80B variants, with the "thinking" mode showing benefits on complex tasks but weaker calibration on simpler ones.
    *   GPT-OSS-120B demonstrates stable reasoning and excellent calibration.

Calibration visualization through curves and histograms is also discussed, suggesting that thresholds should be adapted to observed confidence distributions.

nodes.title: Per-Model Analysis
nodes.summary:
This partial document focuses on evaluating and calibrating the confidence scores of Large Language Models (LLMs) for automated assessment. Key points covered include:

*   **Model Performance Comparison:** Tables present the performance metrics (Accuracy, Expected Calibration Error (ECE), Brier Score, AUC-ROC) of different LLMs (GPT-OSS-120B, Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen3-80B) across various datasets (RiceChem, SciEntsBank, Beetle), with a focus on self-reported confidence.
*   **Reasoning Level Analysis:** Table 6 specifically analyzes GPT-OSS-120B's performance across different reasoning levels (High, Medium, Low) to understand how reasoning depth affects calibration.
*   **Calibration Visualization:** Section 4.3 describes the use of calibration curves and confidence histograms to visually assess the calibration behavior of LLMs, highlighting that confidence scores are often top-skewed.
*   **Per-Model Analysis:** Section 4.4 delves into specific model behaviors, comparing the "Thinking" versus "Instruct" variants of Qwen3-80B to illustrate tradeoffs between accuracy and calibration, and highlighting GPT-OSS-120B's superior calibration and stability across reasoning levels.
*   **Practical Implications for Deployment:** Section 4.5 discusses how well-calibrated confidence can enable selective automation, where high-confidence predictions are processed automatically, but notes limitations on the coverage achievable under strict reliability targets.
*   **Conclusion:** The conclusion summarizes the main findings, emphasizing that self-reported confidence is the most calibrated signal among the tested methods for automated assessment, larger models offer steadier accuracy gains, confidence scores are top-skewed, and these findings support using self-reported confidence as an "automation gate" with an understanding of its practical limitations.

nodes.title: Practical Implications
nodes.summary: This partial document discusses the performance of large language models (LLMs) in terms of calibration, particularly focusing on self-reported confidence as a signal for reliability. It highlights that GPT-OSS-120B significantly outperforms other large models in calibration metrics like ECE, Brier score, and AUC. The document also emphasizes the remarkable stability of GPT-OSS-120B's performance across different reasoning levels, suggesting its robustness for deployment. Practical implications for selective automation are explored, where high-confidence predictions are processed automatically, but it's noted that strict reliability targets limit the share of predictions that can be automated. The conclusion summarizes key findings: self-reported confidence is the most calibrated signal, larger models offer steadier accuracy gains but calibration is method- and dataset-dependent, and confidence scores are top-skewed, requiring relative thresholding. The work aims to provide trustworthy practical guidance for using LLM confidence signals.

structure.title: Conclusion
structure.summary:
This partial document discusses the evaluation of Large Language Models (LLMs) for automated assessment, focusing on their confidence signals and calibration. Key points include:

*   **GPT-OSS-120B Performance:** GPT-OSS-120B significantly outperforms other large models in terms of calibration metrics (ECE, Brier score) and AUC, especially under self-reported confidence. It demonstrates remarkable stability across different reasoning levels, suggesting robustness for deployment.
*   **Practical Implications of Calibration:** Well-calibrated confidence allows for selective automation, where high-confidence predictions are processed automatically, and uncertain cases are flagged for human review. However, even with strict reliability targets, selective automation covers a modest share of predictions.
*   **Key Findings on Confidence Signals:**
    *   Self-reported confidence is the most calibrated signal in the evaluated settings, outperforming sampling-based alternatives with lower inference costs.
    *   Larger models show steadier accuracy gains, but calibration improvements are dataset and method-dependent.
    *   Confidence scores are typically top-skewed, necessitating threshold setting relative to their observed distributions rather than a midpoint.
*   **Conclusion:** The document concludes that self-reported confidence is a suitable "automation gate" for LLM-based assessment, while acknowledging the limitations in the proportion of predictions that meet strict reliability targets. The findings are supported by statistical analyses.
*   **References:** A list of academic references is provided, covering topics such as false discovery rate control, verification of probabilistic forecasts, automatic short answer grading, calibration of neural networks, and various LLM evaluation studies.
